title: For such a time (Esther 4:14)
hookLine: a Jewish queen risks her life for her people; Jews keep Purim remembering it
carry: for such a time as this
last: EVEN EXILE IS NOT THE END.

lines: GO IN UNCALLED, AND YOU MAY DIE.
cards: Far from Jerusalem, in the Persian royal city of Shushan, Jews are still scattered across the empire.
A young Jewish woman, Esther, raised by her cousin Mordecai, has become queen, and she has kept quiet about who her people are.
Then a powerful official, Haman, angry that Mordecai won't bow to him, gets the king to sign an order to destroy the Jews of the whole empire on a single day. He picks the day by casting lots.
Mordecai sends word to the palace: go to the king. Esther sends word back: anyone who walks in uncalled is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter.

teach.b: Mordecai doesn't flatter her. The palace won't hide her, he says, and then: "For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place."
Help will come from somewhere; will she be part of it?

teach.h: FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.
teach.b: Then: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" He doesn't claim to be sure. He asks her to consider that her strange place, a Jewish orphan in a Persian crown, might not be an accident.
Esther asks the Jews of the city to fast for her three days, and she and her maids will fast too.
Then: "so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." She goes in. The king holds out the scepter.
In a reversal, Haman ends up on the gallows he built for Mordecai, and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves.

teach.h: PURIM: THE DAYS OF THE LOT.
teach.b: "They called these days Purim after the name of Pur," and Pur, the text says, means the lot Haman cast.
The book asks for days of feasting and joy, sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor, and Jewish tradition keeps Purim by reading the scroll of Esther aloud.

Some readers point out that in this book, as the King James Bible prints it, God is never named. Yet Jewish and Christian readers have long heard God at work behind it, through a cousin's question and a queen's nerve.

how: Christians read Esther as scripture and sometimes quote Mordecai's for such a time as this when someone takes on a hard calling; Jews keep Purim each year by reading the scroll of Esther aloud, sending food to friends and giving gifts to the poor.

s: Purim is named for the lot Haman cast
"they called these days Purim after the name of Pur" (Esther 9:26), and Pur means the lot (3:7).
Esther was summoned to the king before she spoke for her people
she went in uncalled, which was not according to the law.
Mordecai says that if Esther stays silent, nobody will save the Jews
he says deliverance will arise from another place. the question is whether she'll be part of it.

o: wait until the king happens to call for you.
ask your people to fast with you, then go in.
send a letter instead and stay safe.
games.why: she asks the Jews of the city to fast three days, then goes in: "and if I perish, I perish." the king holds out the golden scepter.

practice: Think of a place where you have access others don't, a boss who listens, a family group chat, a friend who trusts you, where one true word could help someone who can't get in the room.
Notice what keeps you quiet, fear or comfort, without deciding anything yet. If you pray, bring that door to God; if you don't, just stand in front of it for a while.

wordCard.voice: Purim. The festival named for the lot Haman cast, kept by Jews to remember how Esther went in to the king and her people were saved.

orig.note: Hebrew: lots, the plural of pur. Esther 3:7 says pur is the lot Haman cast to choose the day.
